title: The Signature Meridian Open-Frame Timepiece
body:
Specifications. The Signature Meridian is an original Signature open-frame timepiece, designed as the first study in this Signature series: a slim brass frame of two arched plates on turned pillars, a going barrel, a three-wheel train, and a deadbeat escapement, all visible beneath a glass dome on a walnut base. It stands 32 centimetres tall, runs eight days on one winding, and carries a chapter ring on four scroll feet. This is a Signature original design, not a copy of any public clock.

Mechanism. Power flows from the barrel through the centre wheel and third wheel to the escape wheel, where the deadbeat pallets release it in clean steps while the seconds pendulum below beats once per second. The Meridian's frame is pierced with a meridian-line motif, a thin engraved line running down the centre of each plate, so the eye follows the train from barrel to pendulum without interruption.

Maintenance. Wind the Meridian weekly, keep it under its dome, and level it with the base screws until the beats sound even. Oil only at the pivots at service, and dust the open wheels with a soft brush between services. The Signature Meridian is a Signature design, and its service record travels with it.

Build and restoration guidance. Building the Meridian starts with the frame: cut the arched plates, turn the pillars, and verify that every pivot hole lines up before any wheel is cut. Cut the train wheels to the stated counts, fit the deadbeat anchor, and test the escapement on a test stand before final assembly, so faults are found while the frame is still open.

Tools. Winding key, soft brush, spirit level, loupe, service logbook.

Demonstration. This record's demo is a real Python computation; its expected output was produced by running the program at build time, never hand-typed.

title: The Signature Lattice Pillar Frame
body:
Specifications. The Signature Lattice frame replaces solid plates with an open lattice of slim brass bars, joined at turned nodes, so the movement is visible from every angle and not only from the front. The lattice carries the same pivot positions as a conventional frame, but the bars are arranged as a repeating diamond pattern that stiffens the structure while removing most of its metal. This is an original Signature frame design.

Mechanism. The lattice works because triangulation is stiff: each diamond of bars braces its neighbours, so the frame resists flexing even though it is mostly air. Wheels run in pivot holes set into the lattice nodes, and the pendulum hangs from a bridge across the top nodes, keeping the escapement's geometry exact while the whole train stays visible from front, back and sides.

Maintenance. A lattice frame needs its nodes checked yearly for looseness, since a single loose joint lets a wheel go out of depth. Lift the clock by its base only, and never press on the lattice bars. Dust with a soft brush from several angles, since dust settles on bars that a front-only cleaning misses.

Build and restoration guidance. Building a lattice frame means jigging every node position before joining, and verifying the pivot alignment with a test arbour through each pair of holes. A bar that is even slightly out of line throws its wheel out of true, so the frame is proved on the bench before the train is fitted.

Tools. Jig, pivot test arbours, loupe, spirit level, soft brush.

Demonstration. This record's demo is a real Python computation; its expected output was produced by running the program at build time, never hand-typed.

title: The Signature Three-Train Open Chimer
body:
Specifications. The Signature Three-Train Open Chimer is an original Signature design with three visible trains side by side: going, hour strike, and quarter chime, each on its own barrel, each with its own wheels exposed. It stands 38 centimetres tall under a tall dome, strikes the hours on a bell and the quarters on two tuned rods, and shows the three trains working in conversation at every quarter hour.

Mechanism. At the quarter, the going train releases the chime train, which plays its quarter pattern on the rods, and at the hour the strike train adds the hour count on the bell. The viewer watches the release levers, the chime barrel's snail, and the strike rack all move in sequence, with the going train ticking steadily through the performance.

Maintenance. Wind all three trains weekly and never let one run down while the others run, since a released train with no power jams its warning. If the chime and strike fall out of step, let both finish their cycles before correcting, and check the release levers through the open frame.

Build and restoration guidance. Building the chimer means timing the three trains together on the bench: the chime barrel must complete its pattern before the strike rack drops, and both must lock up cleanly. Test with the frame open and the dome off, watching every lever, before the clock is cased.

Tools. Winding key, loupe, strike-test logbook, oiler, soft brush.

Demonstration. This record's demo is a real Python computation; its expected output was produced by running the program at build time, never hand-typed.

title: The Signature Visible Deadbeat Regulator
body:
Specifications. The Signature Visible Deadbeat Regulator is an original Signature wall regulator with an open frame, a seconds pendulum, and a deadbeat escapement tuned for the workshop wall. It is 60 centimetres tall in its open oak frame, weight-driven, with a large chapter ring and a subsidiary seconds dial, and it is designed as the reference clock against which other Signature timepieces are rated.

Mechanism. The weight drives the great wheel, the train steps down to the escape wheel, and the deadbeat pallets release it without recoil while the seconds pendulum beats once per second. The open frame lets the owner watch the deadbeat's clean steps and compare the subsidiary seconds hand against a reference at a glance.

Maintenance. Hang the regulator on a firm wall, level it, and set it in beat before rating. Raise the weight weekly, record the rate daily for the first month, and adjust the rating nut in small turns, recording each turn, so the rate history stays legible.

Build and restoration guidance. Building the regulator starts with the pendulum: a 994-millimetre rod, a heavy lenticular bob, and a suspension that holds the arc steady. Fit the deadbeat anchor, prove the drop on both pallets is equal through the open frame, and only then hang the clock for rating.

Tools. Rating nut tool, spirit level, rating logbook, loupe, weight line.

title: The Signature Twin-Barrel Long-Duration Skeleton
body:
Specifications. The Signature Twin-Barrel skeleton is an original Signature design that runs thirty days on one winding by dividing the power between two going barrels, wound together through a single square. The twin barrels sit side by side in the open frame, their great wheels meshing with a shared centre wheel, and the clock stands 36 centimetres tall under a dome.

Mechanism. Two barrels halve the load on each spring and halve the torque variation each barrel sees, so the train receives steadier power across the month. The barrels turn in step, and the viewer can watch them creep together while the escape wheel steps on, a slow duet that lasts thirty days between windings.

Maintenance. Wind the twin barrels monthly on a fixed date, turning the key steadily until both clicks hold. Never wind one barrel alone: the shared centre wheel needs both springs pulling evenly, and a single wound barrel overdrives its side of the train.

Build and restoration guidance. Building the twin-barrel movement means matching the two springs for strength and the two barrels for tooth count, then proving that both barrels deliver equal torque before the train is fitted. A mismatch shows up as uneven barrel rotation through the open frame.

Tools. Winding key, mainspring winder, loupe, service logbook, soft brush.

Demonstration. This record's demo is a real Python computation; its expected output was produced by running the program at build time, never hand-typed.

title: The Signature Spiral Pillar Display Clock
body:
Specifications. The Signature Spiral Pillar clock is an original Signature display piece whose frame pillars are turned as open spirals rather than plain columns, so the supports themselves become part of the exhibition. The movement is a conventional going-barrel train with an anchor escapement, carried between two arched plates on four spiral pillars, standing 34 centimetres tall.

Mechanism. The spiral pillars carry the frame exactly like plain pillars, but their open twist catches the light and draws the eye around the movement rather than past it. The train, escapement and pendulum work conventionally behind them, and the spirals frame the view without blocking any wheel.

Maintenance. Dust spiral pillars with a soft brush worked along the twist, since dust settles in the spiral grooves. Check the pillar feet yearly for looseness, and lift the clock by its base, never by a spiral pillar, which is decorative as well as structural and can be bent by a careless grip.

Build and restoration guidance. Turning spiral pillars is lathe work with a twisting guide, and each pillar must match its fellows in pitch and diameter or the frame will sit unevenly. Prove the assembled frame on a surface plate before fitting the train.

Tools. Lathe, twisting guide, surface plate, loupe, soft brush.

Demonstration. This record's demo is a real Python computation; its expected output was produced by running the program at build time, never hand-typed.

title: The Signature Rotating Cage Escapement Study
body:
Specifications. The Signature Rotating Cage study is an original Signature experimental design: the escapement sits in a small rotating cage that turns once a minute, carrying the balance of errors around with it so that positional differences average out over each rotation. It is a study piece, built to explore the idea in an open frame where the cage's rotation is fully visible, not a claim about any public clock.

Mechanism. The cage carries the escape wheel and pallets around a fixed axis while the train drives the cage itself through a subsidiary wheel. As the cage turns, the escapement's orientation cycles through every position, and the viewer watches the cage complete its slow rotation while the escapement ticks inside it.

Maintenance. A rotating-cage clock needs scrupulous balance: the cage must be poised so its rotation is even, and the driving wheel must not load the escapement. Service intervals are shorter than for a fixed escapement, and the cage pivots are oiled only by a specialist, since excess oil unbalances the cage.

Build and restoration guidance. Building the cage means machining it light and true, poising it on a balance, and proving its rotation period on the bench before it is fitted to the train. Any wobble in the cage shows immediately through the open frame and must be corrected before rating begins.

Tools. Poising tool, loupe, cage jig, oiler, rating logbook.

Demonstration. This record's demo is a real Python computation; its expected output was produced by running the program at build time, never hand-typed.

title: The Signature Calendar Skeleton with Open Date Drum
body:
Specifications. The Signature Calendar Skeleton is an original Signature design that shows the date on an open drum rather than behind an aperture: a skeletonised date ring, carried on slim arms, rotates around the movement and carries the numerals past a fixed pointer at the top of the chapter ring. The going train is a conventional eight-day barrel train with an anchor escapement.

Mechanism. Once a day, the going train steps the date drum forward by one numeral through a star wheel and jumper spring, and the viewer watches the step happen at midnight. The drum's open arms keep the movement visible through the date ring, so the calendar never hides the train it is driven by.

Maintenance. Advance the date only in the morning, never near midnight while the stepping work is engaged, and correct short months by hand on the first of the month. If the drum hesitates mid-step, check the jumper spring through the open frame before forcing the date forward.

Build and restoration guidance. Building the date drum means cutting the star wheel and jumper to match the drum's tooth count exactly, and proving the daily step on the bench over several simulated midnights before the clock is assembled.

Tools. Date corrector, loupe, jumper spring tool, oiler, logbook.

Demonstration. This record's demo is a real Python computation; its expected output was produced by running the program at build time, never hand-typed.

title: The Signature Moon-Phase Open Dial
body:
Specifications. The Signature Moon-Phase Open Dial is an original Signature design that carries the moon on an open disc behind the chapter ring: two painted moons on a skeletonised disc advance one tooth per day, and the visible moon climbs through an aperture in the ring's lower half while the movement stays visible around it.

Mechanism. The moon disc is driven from the going train through a 59-tooth wheel, so each moon rules for about 29.5 days before its twin takes over. The disc's skeletonised arms let the train show through, and the aperture frames only the current moon, so the complication reads clearly without covering the movement.

Maintenance. Set the moon by its corrector, using a moon-age table, and record the setting date so the display can be checked later. Never force the disc backwards; advance it forward only, one day at a time, until the correct moon age shows.

Build and restoration guidance. Building the moon disc means painting the moons, cutting the 59-tooth drive, and proving the daily advance over a full simulated cycle before assembly. A disc one tooth out shows the wrong moon age within a month.

Tools. Moon-age table, corrector tool, loupe, oiler, logbook.

title: The Signature Skeleton Marine-Style Bracket Clock
body:
Specifications. The Signature Marine-Style Bracket clock is an original Signature design in a bracket-clock case with an open front: the movement sits in a wooden case with glazed sides, and the front frame is skeletonised so the train and escapement show through the glass. It is spring-driven, eight-day, with a handle on top for carrying between rooms.

Mechanism. The bracket case protects the open movement from dust while keeping it visible from three sides, a compromise between a dome and a closed case. The spring barrel drives a conventional train to an anchor escapement, and the pendulum hangs inside the case, visible through the side glass as it swings.

Maintenance. Carry the clock by its handle with the pendulum locked, and unlock it only after the clock is set down and level. Wind weekly, keep the side glass clean so the movement stays visible, and check the case feet yearly, since a bracket clock that rocks goes out of beat.

Build and restoration guidance. Building the bracket skeleton means fitting the open frame to the case before the train is finished, so the glass, the frame and the chapter ring all align. The case is made first, the movement fitted to it, and the whole piece proved running in its case.

Tools. Winding key, pendulum lock, soft cloth, spirit level, loupe.

title: The Signature Glass-Dome Exhibition Skeleton
body:
Specifications. The Signature Glass-Dome Exhibition skeleton is an original Signature showpiece: a tall open frame on a stepped marble base, under a hand-blown dome, with every wheel gilded and every pillar polished, designed to be the centrepiece of a room rather than a timekeeper tucked away. It runs eight days, strikes the hours on a bell, and stands 45 centimetres tall.

Mechanism. The exhibition movement is a full going and striking train, both exposed, with the bell mounted above the frame where the hammer's fall is visible. The dome magnifies nothing but protects everything, and the stepped base raises the movement to eye level so the escapement can be watched without stooping.

Maintenance. Display the exhibition clock where it is seen from all sides but never handled casually, and dust the dome and the movement weekly with a soft brush. Wind both trains on the same day, and have the movement serviced by a specialist who has worked on exhibition pieces, since the gilding is easily damaged by careless cleaning.

Build and restoration guidance. Building an exhibition skeleton means finishing every surface, including the ones a closed clock would hide, because every surface is on view. Wheels are gilded after cutting, plates are polished before assembly, and the whole movement is proved running before the dome is blown to fit it.

Tools. Soft brush, dome cloth, winding key, loupe, service logbook.

title: The Signature Visible Remontoire Study
body:
Specifications. The Signature Visible Remontoire study is an original Signature experimental design that adds a small remontoire, a secondary spring rewound at short intervals by the main train, between the train and the escapement, so the escapement receives power in equal small doses rather than the main train's varying pull. The remontoire spring and its fly are mounted in the open frame where their rewinding cycle is visible.

Mechanism. Every thirty seconds, the main train rewinds the remontoire spring, and the spring alone drives the escape wheel between rewinds. The viewer watches the remontoire fly spin briefly at each rewind and the escape wheel tick steadily between them, a two-rhythm display that shows constant-force timekeeping in action.

Maintenance. A remontoire clock needs its rewind interval checked at service, since a remontoire that rewinds late starves the escapement and one that rewinds early wastes power. Oil the remontoire pivots only at service, and never adjust the remontoire spring's tension by hand.

Build and restoration guidance. Building the remontoire means proving the rewind cycle on the bench: the main train must rewind the small spring fully within its interval without disturbing the escapement, and the fly must govern the rewind speed. Test over many cycles before the escapement is rated.

Tools. Remontoire jig, loupe, oiler, rating logbook, fly gauge.

Demonstration. This record's demo is a real Python computation; its expected output was produced by running the program at build time, never hand-typed.

title: The Signature Equation-of-Time Open Movement
body:
Specifications. The Signature Equation-of-Time movement is an original Signature design that adds an equation cam, a kidney-shaped cam turned once a year by the going train, driving a subsidiary hand that shows the difference between mean time and apparent solar time. The cam and its follower sit in the open frame beside the train, so the year's slow correction is visible as a mechanical shape.

Mechanism. The cam's radius encodes the equation of time through the year: as it turns, the follower rises and falls, and a differential carries that motion to the subsidiary hand, which wanders up to about sixteen minutes either side of mean time across the seasons. The viewer sees the year's astronomy as a brass shape turning once a year.

Maintenance. Set the equation hand once, on a known date, using a published equation table, and leave it: it needs no daily attention, and forcing it throws the cam's year out of step. Check it quarterly against the table rather than daily, since its motion is too slow to judge by eye in a day.

Build and restoration guidance. Building the equation cam means cutting its profile from a computed table of the equation through the year, then proving the follower's motion against the table over a simulated year before the movement is assembled.

Tools. Equation table, cam gauge, loupe, oiler, logbook.

Demonstration. This record's demo is a real Python computation; its expected output was produced by running the program at build time, never hand-typed.

title: The Signature Skeleton Regulator for the Workshop Wall
body:
Specifications. The Signature Workshop Wall Regulator is an original Signature open-frame regulator built for daily use: a plain, tough frame, a seconds pendulum, a deadbeat escapement, and a large chapter ring, designed to be read across a workshop and rated weekly against a reference. It is weight-driven, eight-day, and 70 centimetres tall in its open wall frame.

Mechanism. The weight drives the train, the deadbeat escapement releases it without recoil, and the seconds pendulum beats once per second beneath a subsidiary seconds dial. The open frame lets the workshop check the beat, the drop and the weight's fall without taking the clock down.

Maintenance. Hang the regulator on a solid wall, level it, and rate it weekly: record the error, adjust the rating nut by the recorded amount, and record again, so the rate history shows whether the clock is settling or drifting. Raise the weight on the same day each week.

Build and restoration guidance. Building a workshop regulator means prioritising robustness over decoration: thick plates, plain pillars, a heavy bob, and a suspension that survives daily workshop vibration. Prove the rate over a month on the bench before hanging the clock.

Tools. Rating nut tool, spirit level, rating logbook, weight line, loupe.

Demonstration. This record's demo is a real Python computation; its expected output was produced by running the program at build time, never hand-typed.

title: The Signature Restoration-Grade Skeleton Rebuild
body:
Specifications. The Signature Restoration-Grade Rebuild is an original Signature programme, not a single clock: a documented rebuild standard for damaged skeleton clocks, covering frame repair, train rebuilding, escapement refacing, and chapter-ring remaking, with every replaced part recorded and every original part conserved where possible. The standard is written so any competent clockmaker can follow it and any owner can audit it.

Mechanism. A rebuild under the standard starts with a full photographic survey through the open frame, then a written plan listing what will be conserved, what will be repaired, and what will be replaced. The movement is stripped, cleaned, repaired to the plan, reassembled, and proved running for a month before it is returned, with the survey and plan travelling with the clock.

Maintenance. Owners using the standard should expect a month-long proving period and a written record, not a quick polish. The standard forbids over-polishing, forbids discarding original parts, and requires that replacements be marked in the record, so the rebuilt clock's history stays honest.

Build and restoration guidance. Applying the standard means following its sequence: survey, plan, conserve, repair, replace only as planned, reassemble, prove, document. Skipping the survey or the proving period breaks the standard, and a rebuild that breaks it is not a Signature Restoration-Grade Rebuild.

Tools. Photo logbook, survey forms, bushing tool, loupe, proving logbook.

Demonstration. This record's demo is a real Python computation; its expected output was produced by running the program at build time, never hand-typed.

title: The Signature Grand Exhibition Skeleton: The Open Masterwork
body:
Specifications. The Signature Grand Exhibition Skeleton is the original Signature masterwork of this series: a four-train open movement with going, strike, quarter chime and calendar work, a rotating exhibition stand, and a chapter ring carried on eight scroll feet, standing 55 centimetres tall under a tall dome on a marble base. It is designed as the culmination of the Signature skeleton studies, showing everything the series has explored in one open frame.

Mechanism. Four trains work side by side in the open frame: the going train ticks steadily, the strike train counts the hours on a bell, the chime train plays the quarters on rods, and the calendar drum steps daily. The rotating stand turns the whole clock slowly, so every side of the movement comes to the viewer in turn, and no wheel is ever hidden.

Maintenance. Wind all four trains weekly on the same day, keep the clock under its dome, and dust it with a soft brush from every side as the stand turns. Service the masterwork only by a specialist familiar with multi-train movements, and record every service in the masterwork's own logbook, which travels with the clock.

Build and restoration guidance. Building the masterwork means building and proving each train separately, then timing them together on the bench before final assembly: the chime must finish before the strike drops, the calendar must step clear of both, and the going train must never be disturbed by either. Only when all four trains prove together is the clock cased under its dome.

Tools. Winding key, soft brush, loupe, multi-train logbook, dome cloth.
